edges.description: Less SAE2 activity is expected to reduce activation of SUMO and its transfer to substrates. A reduction in global SUMOylation has not been measured in patient cells in the cited sources.
Tests whether patient missense alleles can replace uba2 function in vivo, which places them with the truncating alleles as loss of function.
edges.limitations: The fish are homozygous null, while patients carry one variant allele, so the model shows what UBA2 is needed for rather than what halving it does; heterozygous fish were not reported to have the phenotype. Wild-type human mRNA rescued only part of the phenotype, and in the full text three of the four patient missense mRNAs, not all, failed to rescue to a significant degree.
edges.source: uba2-null zebrafish with human mRNA rescue

edges.description: uba2 is expressed in the developing pectoral fins and the null fish have abnormal fins, the fish counterpart of the limb defect.
edges.limitations: Fins are not autopods, so the fin defect does not show a split hand or foot; it shows only that uba2 is needed for appendage development, and in a homozygous null rather than at patient dosage.
edges.source: uba2-null zebrafish with human mRNA rescue

edges.description: Lowers SUMOylation directly with an E1 inhibitor and records the developmental consequences.
edges.limitations: The inhibitor blocks the whole SUMO E1 enzyme for a short embryonic window, whereas patients carry a lifelong heterozygous UBA2 variant; the size of the SUMOylation reduction in the embryos is not reported in the abstract, and the drug may have effects beyond SUMO E1.

edges.description: Embryo transcriptomics show repression of neural crest differentiation genes after SUMOylation inhibition; this is the evidence behind the neural crest hypothesis.
edges.limitations: The readout is gene expression in drug-treated embryos; differentiation of neural crest cells themselves was not shown in the abstract, and no human UBA2 carrier tissue has been examined.

edges.description: Offspring of treated dams have syndactyly, a digit malformation seen in ACCES syndrome.
edges.limitations: Syndactyly, not split hand or foot, is reported, so the model reproduces part of the digital spectrum but not ectrodactyly.

nodes.description: Uba2 is strongly expressed in the developing mouse limb bud and uba2 in zebrafish pectoral fins. Reduced UBA2 activity disturbs formation of the central rays of the hands and feet, giving split hand or split foot, syndactyly and other digit anomalies. The patterning step that UBA2 affects (for example maintenance of the central apical ectodermal ridge) has not been identified.

nodes.description: In mouse embryos exposed to a SUMO E1 inhibitor, genes driving neural crest differentiation are repressed, and the offspring have craniofacial deformities. Neural crest cells form much of the facial skeleton, so this step is proposed to link reduced SUMOylation to the facial features of ACCES syndrome. It has not been shown in human UBA2 carriers.

nodes.description: The UBA2-SAE1 heterodimer is the only E1 enzyme for SUMO, so reduced UBA2 activity is expected to lower SUMO conjugation of developmental transcription factors and chromatin regulators. Complete loss of SUMOylation is embryonic lethal; the partial reduction from a single affected allele is compatible with life but disturbs the development of the scalp skin, the distal limbs and other tissues.

nodes.description: Pregnant mice given the selective SUMO E1 inhibitor TAK-981 during the early post-implantation stage. A high dose is embryonic lethal; lower doses give viable offspring with craniofacial deformities, hydrocephalus, syndactyly and an aplasia cutis-like skin defect, and the treated embryos show repressed neural crest differentiation genes. No genetic Uba2 heterozygous mouse phenotype has been reported.

nodes.description: Heterozygous truncating, splice-site and missense UBA2 variants reduce the activity of SAE2, the catalytic subunit of the UBA2-SAE1 SUMO-activating E1 enzyme. Truncating alleles are predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay, and human missense alleles fail to rescue uba2-null zebrafish, so the published mechanism is loss of function. Whole-gene deletion of UBA2 in the 19q13.11 deletion syndrome gives overlapping features, consistent with haploinsufficiency. No dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect has been reported.

nodes.description: Homozygous uba2 knockout zebrafish develop small eyes, microcephaly, mandibular hypoplasia, abnormal fins and deficient growth, and die by 12 days post fertilization. Injected wild-type human UBA2 mRNA partly rescues the gross phenotype, while mRNAs carrying patient missense variants rescue it less well, which is the main functional evidence that the missense alleles lose function.
